bounds: Two concurrent calls, three initial entries and one concurrent old-writer append, batch size two, matching/unavailable receipts and bounded cursor revisions. Separate serial reliable-progress case has three invocations. Separate list-isolation case has three legacy queues and a persistent first-queue removal failure.
limitations: Two concurrent adoption calls, three initial retained entries (two valid and one malformed), one valid old-writer append, original marker cleanup racing adoption, a two-entry batch and digest ranks rather than cryptographic strings. The conflict case uses an unmatched receipt to represent provider, event, payload or historical digest conflicts.

KV adoption never removes raw entries because this owner has no durable fence proving old writers quiescent. The model includes one concurrent old-writer append; an explicit negative witness demonstrates how unfenced stale KV read/modify/write deletion would lose it. Redis LREM is atomic. This does not prove old writers safe against each other.

Retained KV raws are replayed against exact durable SQL receipts without reopening completed work. Cleanup of retained KV entries requires an existing owner with a separately proved writer fence and is not implemented here. KV eventual visibility and durability are external assumptions, not proved by the local namespace fixture.

The SQL transaction and exact payload/terminal receipt predicates are abstracted as matching, absent or unavailable. A missing historical receipt is quarantined, never inserted or treated as undelivered. PGlite exercises real SQL; PostgreSQL checks actual row-lock waiting, concurrent cursor reservation and retention racing adoption. The production KV adapter exercises retained read-only adoption and isolated loopback Redis exercises atomic removal; TypeScript refinement and production provider behavior are not proved.

Cursor reservations advance only selection hints. Losing a cursor reply or a progress CAS cannot authorize removal. The SQL receipt, not cursor position, is required before LREM. Scope includes the configured backend/environment and one legacy queue.

Production limits attempts to 25 per list and uses a separate one-second per-list work budget. The model abstracts this as one or two attempted entries. Full KV-array reads and hashing remain unbounded by the work timer, and a single in-flight SQL or cache call can outlive it.

The serial progress case assumes a fixed three-entry snapshot, available SQL and original matching markers, three fair cron invocations and returning operations. It establishes transfer of the two valid entries despite a permanent poison entry and one-attempt budgets; it does not promise unconditional backlog clearance or resolution of unavailable historical receipts. The separate three-list progress case assumes each operation returns, but permits a persistent removal failure on the first queue; retained receipts permit the later queues and SQL drain to proceed.

Outbox handler effects, Stripe signature verification, billing idempotency and retention are separate protocols. StripeDeliveryOutbox retains its existing lease model; a durable handoff here is not proof of end-to-end external delivery.

Identical raw multiplicity and SHA256 collisions are outside the set abstraction. Actual tests preserve identical copies until a matching receipt and remove them individually; collision resistance is assumed. Unknown or malformed raws remain retained for operator reconciliation with payload-free diagnostics.

Legacy handoff flags are set under the same row lock as matching adoption and prevent both current webhook cleanup variants from deleting the exact receipt. A row-level BEFORE DELETE guard also retains it under old unfiltered cleanup SQL and direct deletes during rolling deployment. Existing receipts already removed before first adoption cannot be reconstructed; their raws require explicit operator reconciliation. The flag is not automatically cleared after Redis removal, because duplicate raws or lost replies may remain. Retained receipt and KV-raw cleanup are unresolved obligations of the existing owner.

assumptions: Each started cursor, SQL and Redis operation eventually returns or fails; weak fairness of Advance is assumed.
Each started cursor, SQL and KV operation eventually returns or fails; weak fairness of Advance is assumed.
Each started operation eventually returns or fails, including explicit unavailable receipt results; weak fairness of Advance is assumed.

One serial cron makes three invocations on a fixed three-entry snapshot with available SQL and original matching receipts. Start, First and Finish are weakly fair; no old producer writes, and at least the first reserved entry is attempted.
One cron visits its three retained legacy queues. SQL succeeds and each remove operation returns, but removal of the first queue always fails. Adopt, Remove and Next are weakly fair.
